newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bonds dive after Fernandez comments.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bonds dive after Fernandez comments.

text.p: Argentine bonds plunged on Friday after a session of volatile trade with comments by Economy Minister Roque Fernandez putting a downer on a surge in the morning.
"Fernandez poured cold water on the buyback speculation," said a trader with a large foreign bank.
The market soared early on the announcement that Argentina will issue a 10-year $750 million global dollar bond to take advantage of favorable market conditions.

But statements by Fernandez that the issue will not be increased and that there are no plans for the time being of a buy back of Brady debt cut off the early rally and profit- taking set in. The dollar-denominated Bocon Previsional 2 due 2001 fell $0.55 to 118.20, while Argentina's FRB due 2005 fell 3/8 to 83-3/4. The dollar-denominated Bocon Provisional due 2007 fell $0.19 to 103.00.
Traders said activity was extremely volatile, particularly with the near u-turn staged by the market after Fernandez statements. A turnaround in U.S. Treasuries added to the poor performance.
The profit-taking that set in came after a surge in prices during the rest of the week on the back of confidence the government is well placed to continue its economic policies.

That was highlighted by an earlier-than-expected Senate passage of the government's tax-hiking measures on Wednesday. The announcement on Thursday of the privatization of mortgage bank Banco Hipotecario helped underline the government's steady line of policy.
"The government is firm in its conviction of its economic policies," said Roberto Costa Bourdieu, senior-fixed income analyst at Banco Rio de la Plata.
The market payed little attention to the 36-hour strike that has plagued the country for two days, particularly because the government has not given in to union demands.
Market players forecast the market could be volatile again next week during the wait for the key U.S. September jobs report on Friday.

The decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve to keep rates steady this week underpinned Argentine bonds and the jobs report will be the first big economic indicator to signal whether or not the Fed's decision was the right one, said traders and analysts.
In the money markets, call money rates fell to 5.88 percent from 5.95 percent.
